title: The Agent-Ready Score
subtitle: A 16-question diagnostic for agency operators before they spend $10K on a build

answers.label: Owner / Founder ,  I sign the build invoice
Ops Lead / COO ,  I run the workflow today
Individual Contributor ,  I do the manual steps

questions.text: When work comes in, is the data captured in structured fields or as free text in email and Slack?

answers.label: Free text in inboxes and chat, no template
A template exists but most people skip it
Form exists, optional fields, no validation
Required fields, light validation, one channel
Structured intake form, required fields, validated, single landing spot

questions.text: How often is critical data missing or wrong on intake, forcing someone to chase the client?

answers.label: Almost every intake needs follow-up
More than half need a follow-up
About a third need clarification
Roughly 1 in 5 needs follow-up
Less than 1 in 10 needs any follow-up

questions.text: Does the same piece of client data live in one place, or is it scattered across 3+ systems?

answers.label: Same info lives in 4+ tools, drift is constant
3 tools hold overlapping data, manual reconciliation
2 tools, one is mostly authoritative
One source of truth, occasional manual sync to a second
One source of truth, other tools sync from it automatically

low.headline: Your intake is too messy to automate
low.text: Before any AI build, the front door has to be fixed. Free-text intakes and scattered data mean the agent will guess and the human will redo the work anyway. Spend the next 30 days here, not on an automation vendor.
steps: Pick one channel (a form or a CRM record) as the only legal way work enters the workflow
Make 5 to 8 fields required with validation, and reject submissions that skip them
Delete or archive the duplicate spots where the same data lives today, leaving one source of truth

mid.headline: Intake works but leaks at the edges
mid.text: You have structure, but the edges (optional fields, side-channel requests, duplicate records) are exactly where the agent will fail in production. Close the 2 to 3 obvious leaks before you build.
steps: Audit the last 20 intakes and list every field that was missing or wrong, then make the top 3 required
Pick the one system that owns each client field, and turn the others into read-only views
Add a single rejection step that bounces incomplete intakes back to the sender automatically

high.headline: Your intake is build-ready
high.text: This is the part most agencies fail. You already have structured, single-source data flowing in, which means an agent can read it without a human translator in the middle. Move on to scoring the next category.
steps: Document the intake schema (field names, types, required vs optional) in one page so a builder can ingest it
Add a lightweight monitor that flags intakes with empty required fields before they hit the workflow
Keep the intake form versioned, so you can roll back if a field change breaks downstream automation

questions.text: If you asked your best person to write down exactly how they decide qualify, scope, or route, could they?

answers.label: I just know ,  pure tacit knowledge
A few rules of thumb, mostly in their head
Partially documented, missing edge cases
Documented rules with named criteria
Documented rules with named criteria and thresholds

questions.text: How often does the same input produce different outputs depending on who is handling it?

answers.label: Different person, different answer, every time
Frequent disagreement on borderline cases
Same answer about 70 percent of the time
Mostly consistent, occasional drift on edge cases
Same input produces the same output regardless of operator

questions.text: What share of the decisions your team makes in this workflow can be expressed as if-then rules versus pure judgment?

answers.label: Almost all judgment, very few rules
Half rules, half judgment
Most cases follow rules, judgment for the rest
Rules cover 80 percent, judgment for clear exceptions
Rules cover 95 percent, judgment only on rare escalations

low.headline: The logic only lives in someone's head
low.text: You cannot automate a decision nobody has written down. Right now an agent would either invent rules or default to a single bland answer. The fix is documentation, not technology.
steps: Shadow your best operator for 5 real cases and write down every decision they made, including the why
Group the decisions into 3 to 5 named criteria with explicit thresholds (not adjectives like big or risky)
Have a second person run the documented rules on 10 historical cases and see where they break

mid.headline: Rules exist but edge cases will sink the build
mid.text: You have a workable rulebook, but the 20 percent of cases that need judgment are exactly the ones an agent will get wrong in front of a client. Tighten the rules or add a human checkpoint.
steps: List the 5 most common exceptions from the last 90 days and decide for each: new rule, or escalate to human
Convert any adjective in your rules (big client, complex scope) into a number you can actually measure
Pick one operator to be the rule owner and give them authority to update the rulebook monthly

high.headline: Your decisions are codifiable
high.text: The rules are written, named, and consistent across operators. That means an agent can apply them with high fidelity and the rare edge case is a clean escalation, not a mystery.
steps: Export the rulebook as structured logic (a decision table or YAML) that a developer can read directly
Define what an escalation looks like, including who it goes to and what data goes with it
Set a quarterly review of the rulebook against the last 100 decisions to catch drift early

questions.text: How wide is the workflow you want to automate?

answers.label: End to end across 4+ departments and many tools
Spans 3 departments with handoffs
One department, several steps, multiple tools
One team, one outcome, 2 to 3 tools
One narrow task with a clearly defined start and finish

questions.text: How varied are the outputs the workflow needs to produce?

answers.label: Every output is bespoke, no two are alike
High variation with some recurring patterns
A handful of templates cover most cases
3 to 5 standard output formats
1 or 2 standard output formats with clear variants

questions.text: How often does this workflow actually run?

answers.label: A few times a quarter
A few times a month
Weekly
Multiple times per week
Daily or many times per day

low.headline: The scope is too wide to build
low.text: You are trying to automate a department, not a task. Every agent build that tries to swallow a whole workflow fails inside 90 days. Cut the scope before you spend a dollar.
steps: Map the full workflow on one page and circle the single step that takes the most human time
Define a start trigger and a finish output for that one step, ignore everything around it
Re-run this scorecard on the narrow step alone and see if the score jumps

mid.headline: Scope is close but needs trimming
mid.text: Your workflow is narrow enough to consider, but the output variation or the cross-team handoffs will add complexity that doubles the build cost. Trim before you build.
steps: Cap the number of output formats the agent supports in v1, push exceptions to a human queue
Remove any step that requires another team to do something, or build that handoff as a separate workflow
Commit to a v1 that handles the 80 percent case and explicitly ignores the rest

high.headline: The scope is tight enough to build
high.text: Narrow task, predictable outputs, runs often enough to matter. This is the shape of a workflow that pays back the build inside 90 days.
steps: Write a one-page spec: trigger, inputs, decision rules, outputs, escalation path
Lock the scope: anything new becomes a v2 ticket, not a v1 change
Estimate the manual hours per month this workflow burns today, that is your payback baseline

questions.text: Is there a clear point in the workflow where a human reviews or approves before something hits a client?

answers.label: No review, work goes straight to the client today
Review happens informally, often skipped under pressure
Review exists but the criteria are vague
Defined review step with a checklist
Defined review step, named owner, clear approve or reject criteria

questions.text: If the agent gets it wrong, how reversible is the mistake?

answers.label: Mistake reaches the client immediately and is hard to undo
Mistake is visible to the client but recoverable with apology
Mistake is caught after the fact during weekly review
Mistake is caught by a downstream check before the client sees it
Mistake is caught at the review step, client never sees it

questions.text: Does the person who would review the agent's output actually have time to do it?

answers.label: No, the reviewer is the bottleneck we are trying to remove
Sometimes, but reviews get rushed or skipped
Yes for low volume, no if we scale
Yes, with the time freed up by the automation itself
Yes, the reviewer has dedicated capacity for this

low.headline: No safety net means no agent
low.text: Without a real review point, an agent's first hallucination goes straight to a client. That is the kind of incident that ends an agent program in week 2. Build the human checkpoint before the build, not after.
steps: Designate one person as the reviewer of record and give them the criteria to approve or reject
Add an explicit pause in the workflow where the agent's output waits for human sign-off
Define what gets escalated, to whom, and within what timeframe

mid.headline: Review exists but is fragile
mid.text: You have a checkpoint, but it leaks under pressure or has vague criteria. Tighten it before adding an agent, otherwise the agent will amplify the leak.
steps: Turn the review into a 5 to 7 item checklist the reviewer must sign off on, no shortcuts
Track review skip rate for 30 days and fix the root cause if it is above 10 percent
Give the reviewer authority to send work back to the agent with reasons, not just approve or reject

high.headline: You have the safety net the build needs
high.text: A named reviewer with capacity and clear criteria is the single best predictor that an agent build will survive past 90 days. This is the foundation most agencies skip.
steps: Instrument the review step so you can measure approve, reject, and edit rates from day 1
Use the first 30 days of review data to tighten the agent's prompts and rules
Move toward sampling-based review once approve rate is consistently above 90 percent

questions.text: What budget have you set aside for this build (design, build, and 90 days of iteration)?

answers.label: Under $2K, hoping to glue it together with Zapier
$2K to $5K, expecting a quick win
$5K to $10K with some runway for fixes
$10K to $25K with budget for iteration
$25K+ with explicit budget for ongoing improvement

questions.text: Who owns this automation after it ships?

answers.label: Nobody decided yet
The founder, on top of everything else
Whoever raises their hand when it breaks
Named owner with other priorities
Named owner with dedicated time to maintain and improve it

questions.text: How will you know in 90 days whether this build paid back?

answers.label: We will just feel it
Vague sense of hours saved
A rough estimate of time freed up
Specific hours per month with a baseline
Hours saved, error rate, and revenue impact, with a baseline measured before the build

questions.text: What happens if the agent breaks for a day in week 3?

answers.label: The business stops, no manual fallback exists
Major scramble, clients notice
Manual fallback is painful but possible
Manual fallback is documented and rehearsed
Manual fallback is in place and the team has run it

low.headline: You are not set up to own this build
low.text: Even a perfect workflow fails without budget, an owner, and a way to measure success. Fix the operational side before you write the first prompt.
steps: Set a realistic budget that includes 90 days of iteration after launch, not just the initial build
Name one person as the owner with explicit time allocated to maintain the agent
Write down the one or two numbers that will tell you in 90 days whether this paid back

mid.headline: You have most of the operational pieces
mid.text: The build can succeed, but the gaps you have (budget, owner, or measurement) are the same ones that make agents quietly rot after launch. Close them before you build.
steps: Lock the success metrics in writing and measure the baseline before any build starts
Give the named owner time on their calendar specifically for agent maintenance, not just on-call
Document the manual fallback and run it once as a fire drill before launch

high.headline: You are ready to own this build
high.text: Budget, owner, metrics, and a fallback. This is the operational profile of an agency that gets paid back inside 90 days and keeps the agent running for years.
steps: Baseline the metric this week so you can prove the payback later, not argue about it
Set a 30, 60, 90 day check-in cadence with the owner before the build kicks off
Pick the single highest-scoring workflow from your assessment and start there, not the loudest one

cta.headline: Want me to score this workflow with you?
cta.description: I run this assessment live with agency operators every week. Bring one workflow, leave with a build plan, a budget, and a payback estimate. No pitch, no slides.
